bib.title: Food-101 – Mining Discriminative Components with Random Forests

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Food-101 – Mining Discriminative Components with Random Forests", Lukas Bossard, Matthieu Guillaumin, Luc Van Gool (ETH Zürich; K.U. Leuven). The extracted text names no venue. ECCV 2014 comes from the caller's brief, not from the PDF text. 16 pages, with no appendix.

COVERAGE: I read all 40,847 of 40,847 characters, pages 1–16, including all three results tables, the MIT-Indoor section, the conclusion and the full reference list (refs 1–40). There is no appendix and no separate limitations section. Figure captions came from figures.py (Figs 1–8). I skipped nothing.

PLAIN ANSWER FIRST: **The paper never measures or reports the noise level of the training set.** It says the training images "still contain some amount of noise" from "intense colors and sometimes wrong labels". It gives no percentage, no audit, and no description of how the test images were cleaned (who did it, what the criteria were, or how many images were removed). If a note says "Food-101's training set has X% label noise", this paper cannot support the X. The paper supports two narrower points. First, the dataset was designed on purpose so that training data is noisy and test data is clean. Second, the authors' stated reason was that real-world systems should cope with weakly labelled data. For a modern multimodal-engineering note, this is a sharpens-level citation at most, for "Reading public benchmarks". Use it to cite where Food-101's train/test asymmetry comes from, and to show that a benchmark's split design is something a reader should check. It does not change or evidence any claim about current VLM or multimodal performance. Its accuracy numbers (pre-2014 AlexNet at 56.40%) are long dated. Part (b), RF component mining, is of historical interest only. Its one durable result is that the CNN beat every hand-built pipeline, including the authors' own.

CLAIMS

- claim: The dataset was built from foodspotting.com user uploads. It covers the top 101 popular, consistently named dishes, with 750 randomly sampled training images and 250 manually cleaned test images per class. Training images were deliberately left uncleaned.
  number: 101 classes; 750 train / 250 test per class
  setup: Images were scraped from a user-photo site where users annotate place and dish type.
  quote: "We chose the top 101 most popular and consistently named dishes and randomly sampled 750 training images. Additionally, 250 test images were collected for each class, and were manually cleaned. On purpose, the training images were not cleaned, and thus still contain some amount of noise. This comes mostly in the form of intense colors and sometimes wrong labels."
  where: p.4, Sect. 3

- claim: The authors' reason for leaving the training labels noisy is that systems should scale with class count while using weakly labelled data.
  number: none
  setup: This is a design rationale. They give no experiment on noise.
  quote: "We believe that real-world computer vision algorithms should be able to cope with such weakly labeled data if they are meant to scale well with the number of classes to recognise."
  where: p.4, Sect. 3

- claim: Images were rescaled to a maximum side of 512 px, and smaller images were excluded, giving 101,000 images in total.
  number: 512 px; 101'000 images
  setup: The 101,000 total equals 101 × 1000, so excluded images must have been replaced or the count is nominal. The paper does not say which.
  quote: "All images were rescaled to have a maximum side length of 512 pixels and smaller ones were excluded from the whole process. This leaves us with a dataset of 101'000 real-world images in total"
  where: p.4–5, Sect. 3

- claim: The paper presents Food-101 as the first public real-world food dataset. The only earlier public set (PFID) is lab-shot fast food.
  number: PFID has 101 classes, 3 instances per class, 8 images per instance
  setup: This is a comparison with prior food datasets.
  quote: "The Pittsburgh food dataset [5] contains 101 classes, but with only 3 instances per class and 8 images per instance."
  where: p.3, Sect. 2

- claim: A CNN (AlexNet architecture, trained from scratch in Caffe) was the best method on Food-101 at 56.40%, beating the paper's own RFDC by 5.64 points. The cost was six days of training on a single GPU.
  number: CNN 56.40%; margin 5.64%; 450,000 iterations; 6 days on a Tesla K20X
  setup: Food-101, 750 train / 250 test per class, metric is average accuracy (the fraction of test images classified correctly).
  quote: "Also on this dataset, cnn set the state of the art and rfdc are outperformed by a margin of 5.64%. This is paid by a considerably longer training time of six days on a nvidia Tesla K20X." / "we train a deep cnn on our dataset using the architecture of [23] as provided by the Caffe [16] library until it converged (450'000 iterations)."
  where: p.12, Sect. 5.3; Table 2 p.10

- claim: Full results on Food-101 (Table 2) are BOW 28.51, IFV 38.88, CNN 56.40, RF 32.72, RCF 28.46, MLDS 42.63, RFDC 50.76.
  number: as listed
  setup: All component-mining methods use 20 components per class. RFDC used 30 trees, max depth 5, and 500 positives per component.
  quote: "Global bow [24] 28.51 ifv [32] 38.88 cnn [23] 56.40 Local rf [3] 32.72 rcf [29] 28.46 mlds (≈ [34]) 42.63 rfdc (this paper) 50.76"
  where: Table 2, p.10

- claim: RFDC beats the MLDS part-mining method and IFV by 8.13 and 11.88 points.
  number: 50.76%; +8.13; +11.88
  setup: Food-101 as above.
  quote: "we measure an accuracy of 50.76%, an improvement of 8.13% and 11.88% compared to mlds and ifv, respectively."
  where: p.12

- claim: Feature choice matters a great deal for RFDC. Combining IFV SURF and colour reaches 49.40%, while HOG reaches only 8.85%.
  number: HOG 8.85; BoW SURF 33.47; BoW SURF+Color 38.83; IFV SURF 44.79; IFV Color 14.24; IFV SURF+Color 49.40
  setup: RFDC with default settings (30 trees, depth 7, top 20 components per class, 100 positives).
  quote: "ifv surf @64 + Color@64 49.40"; "- hog 8.85"
  where: Table 1, p.10

- claim: RFDC is robust to its forest hyperparameters. Accuracy plateaus beyond about 4 levels of depth, above 200 positives per model, and above about 20 components per class. Moving from 20 to 50 components raises feature dimensionality from 42,420 to 106,050.
  number: 42'420 → 106'050
  setup: Food-101, varying one parameter at a time (Fig. 5).
  quote: "from 42'420 for 20 components, the dimensionality reaches 106'050 for 50 components and thus heavily impacts memory usage and speed."
  where: p.10

- claim: On MIT-Indoor, RFDC gets 54.40% with the restricted training set and 58.36% with the full training set. That is below DMS (64.03) and below IFV (60.77).
  number: 54.40 / 58.36 vs DMS 64.03, IFV 60.77, IFV+DMS 66.87
  setup: 50 components per class, horizontally flipped training images, about 80 train / 20 test images per class.
  quote: "using 50 components per class our method yields 54.40% and 58.36% average accuracy for the restricted and full training set, respectively."
  where: p.13, Table 3 p.14

- claim: Compute costs are about 250 CPU hours to train and about 0.8 s per image to classify on 8 cores.
  number: 250 CPU h; 0.8 s; 55% of training time spent on the forest; 70% of inference time spent on encoding
  setup: Full pipeline, reported in the MIT-Indoor section.
  quote: "our full pipeline uses around 250 cpu hours" / "the full classification time (including feature extraction and Fisher encoding) of one image is around 0.8 seconds using 8 cores, where 70% of the time is spent on encoding"
  where: p.14

- claim: The authors argue that Food-101 has a bias unlike other benchmarks, because part-based RFDC beats IFV on it.
  number: none
  setup: An interpretive claim, not tested.
  quote: "Our Food-101 dataset (where rfdc outperforms ifv) therefore presents a bias significantly different from available sets, highlighting its interest as a novel benchmark."
  where: p.14

- claim: The errors they report come from visual similarity, clutter and ambiguity.
  number: none
  setup: Qualitative, from Fig. 8.
  quote: "Confusions are often because of visual similarity (onion rings vs. french fries, carrot cake vs. chocolate cake), clutter (prime rib vs. spring roll) or ambiguous examples (steak vs. risotto)."
  where: p.13

LIMITS:
- The training-set noise is never quantified. There is no estimate of the label-error rate and no audit sample.
- The test-set cleaning procedure is not described: no annotators, criteria, or count of images removed.
- There is no experiment on how training-label noise affects accuracy, for example clean versus noisy training data.
- There is no validation split for Food-101. A 200,000-superpixel validation set is carved out of the training superpixels for mining only.
- There are no error bars and no repeated runs. Each figure comes from a single run.
- The CNN baseline was AlexNet trained from scratch, with no ImageNet pretraining mentioned and no tuning reported.
- The authors concede the CNN beats them, and that the MIT-Indoor results trail DMS and IFV.
- Dated: every number predates pretrained CNNs and transfer learning. The accuracy figures do not describe current multimodal systems.

BUILDS ON: Random forests, Ho (1995) and Breiman (2001). RF with linear-split image classification, Bosch, Zisserman, Munoz (2007). Improved Fisher Vectors, Sánchez et al. (2013). Mid-level discriminative patches, Singh, Gupta, Efros (2012), which is the MLDS baseline. Doersch, Gupta, Efros (2013). Juneja et al., Blocks That Shout (2013). Randomized clustering forests, Moosmann, Nowak, Jurie (2008). Graph-based superpixels, Felzenszwalb & Huttenlocher (2004). SURF, Bay et al. (2006). Spatial pyramids, Lazebnik et al. (2006). The CNN, Krizhevsky et al. (2012), run in Caffe (Jia 2013). Cutting-plane structural SVMs, Joachims et al. (2009), run in DLib (King 2009). PFID, Chen et al. (2009). MIT-Indoor, Quattoni & Torralba (2009).

CODE: none. The paper includes only equations: information gain (Eq. 1), the SVM split (Eq. 2), leaf-averaged class confidence (Eq. 3), and leaf distinctiveness (Eq. 4), on pp.6–7. The dataset URL is printed on p.5: http://www.vision.ee.ethz.ch/datasets/food-101/

FIGURES:
- Fig. 2 (p.4), "one example for 100 out of the 101 classes… Note the high variance in food type, color, exposure and level of detail, but also visually and semantically similar food types." In one glance it shows how varied the classes are and how close some of them look.
- Fig. 6 (p.11), per-class accuracy for IFV versus RFDC across the best, worst, most improved and degraded classes. It shows that a single aggregate accuracy figure hides a wide per-class spread, which could help a benchmark-reading note.
- Fig. 8 (p.13), confidence heat maps for correct and confused pairs. It shows the confusion types faster than prose does.
- Figs 3 and 4 (pp.5, 8) are pipeline diagrams, useful only if the method itself is taught.

PROBLEMS: pypdf raised repeated "Multiple definitions in dictionary … /ExtGState" warnings, which did not affect the text. Small ligature and diacritic artefacts appear (Z¨ urich, Sánchez rendered as S´ anchez). Table 2 and Table 3 were flattened into running text, and I re-associated the values by order. The flattened text of Table 3 interleaves two columns, but the values match the prose. There were no embedded instructions. The venue is not stated anywhere in the extracted text.
